label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Peter, I don’t want to wave away your payroll experience. Nine years of running payroll gives you a much better view of the recovery and forecasting problems than someone who only sees the compassionate side of an advance request. On Brenda’s **current informal arrangement**, I think you and her Finance Manager have valid concerns: no written limit, repeated monthly use, and approval through a conversation in HR is not a sustainable system. The leaver risk is real too.

Where I disagree is with the conclusion that closing the window altogether is necessarily the lower-risk option. We tried almost exactly that approach in 2025 and ended up reversing it.

We have around 340 staff across Embakasi and Changamwe, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We closed advances in February 2025 after Finance pushed back, using almost the same arguments you have set out. We gave two months’ notice and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO. This was not an abrupt closure with no preparation.

In the six months after closure, calls to our office from debt collectors and loan apps went from a handful to **61 calls logged by reception**. Those were 61 calls, not necessarily 61 different employees, but the change was impossible to ignore. Some apps were calling supervisors who had been listed as “referees”, so what looked like an employee’s private borrowing arrangement became an operational and workplace issue.

Unplanned absence also rose on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least **three missed Mombasa runs** to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. I would not claim that every absence or collector call was caused by closing advances; there is no clean way to prove that. But the pattern was enough to show me that the need had not disappeared. It had moved somewhere less visible and, in some cases, considerably more damaging.

The case that stayed with me was a loader at Changamwe. By the time he came to me, he was using **six loan apps at once**, borrowing from one to pay another. It took four months of working with him and payroll to unwind it. Nothing in our financial literacy session had equipped him to deal with that spiral once he was inside it.

I also think the SACCO alternative needs a practicality test. Our SACCO loans generally take **two to three weeks** to process and require guarantors. They can be useful for a planned expense. They are not much use when a child is sent home over fees on a Tuesday. And for somebody earning around **KES 28,000 a month**, the difficulty is not always a lack of budgeting knowledge. There may simply be very little room to absorb an emergency, however well the person understands money.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but not by returning to the informal system. The policy now provides for:

- a maximum advance of **40% of net pay**;
- only **one advance per pay cycle**;
- repayment **in full at the next payroll**, rather than rolling the balance forward;
- **no fee or interest**; and
- requests through the **payroll portal**, not through my office.

Before approving, payroll also checks the other deductions so that the total remains within the Employment Act’s overall **two-thirds-of-wages deduction limit**. The combined effect of the cap and that check is important: nobody should reach month-end with nothing left.

Since reopening, we have had roughly **55–70 requests a month**, averaging around **KES 9,000**. Apart from two leavers, recovery has been **100%**. The total written off for the year was approximately **KES 14,000**. So your warning about people leaving while owing money did happen to me—but, in my case, its actual cost was very small and measurable.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. The difference is that he can see its limits and forecast the payroll effect. There is a fixed ceiling, a defined repayment point and a visible request process. It is no longer an unknown number of discretionary payments appearing around the forecast.

The administration point also deserves a fair comparison. You are right that time spent approving advances is real HR time, which is why I would not ask Brenda to keep running requests from her office. But the costs of closure do not disappear simply because they are harder to assign. With us, reception absorbed collector calls, supervisors spent time dealing with collectors and distressed staff, fleet dealt with missed runs, and operations dealt with post-month-end absence. Those costs were spread across departments, while the advance write-off sat neatly in one Finance schedule. I cannot produce a precise shilling figure for all the disruption, so I would not invent one. But it should not be valued at zero merely because it is scattered.

Brenda, for your meeting on the 18th, I would therefore avoid arguing for or against “advances” in the abstract. Your present arrangement and a properly controlled scheme are not the same thing. You could put a proposal to Finance along these lines:

1. **Replace the informal practice with a written, no-fee salary-advance policy.**
2. **Cap it at up to 40% of net pay**, or a lower starting percentage if that is what Finance needs for a pilot.
3. **Allow one advance per pay cycle**, with no top-ups.
4. **Recover it in full at the next payroll**, subject to the statutory deduction check, so it does not become a continuing loan book.
5. **Route requests through payroll**, with a clear cut-off and standard approval rules. HR handles exceptions and employee support; HR does not become the lender’s front desk.
6. **Track repeat monthly use**, because Peter is right that permanently living one month behind is a problem. Repeated use should trigger support or referral, not simply another unexamined approval.
7. **Review it after six months** using request volumes and values, recovery, repeat use, administration time, collector calls and absence immediately after month-end.

The SACCO and financial literacy can remain part of that proposal. I would present them as complements, not substitutes: the SACCO for needs that fit its processing time, and literacy support for people showing signs of recurring difficulty.

That gives Finance something concrete to assess and gives you measurements with which to revisit the decision. It also directly addresses the legitimate objections without assuming that the alternatives are cost-free. If the capped scheme produces the dependency Peter predicts, your own review will show it. If external collection calls and operational disruption fall instead, Finance should see that evidence too.

So, Peter, I agree with much of your diagnosis of an uncapped, discretionary scheme. I just do not think “notice, SACCO, literacy session, close” is always the responsible cure. In my case, some staff did adjust after closure—but they adjusted by borrowing elsewhere, and part of the consequences came back through my gates anyway. A tightly limited advance is not a complete answer to low wages or financial distress. It can, however, be a considerably safer bridge than either an informal HR favour or six loan apps.
